cultivar: Bulang Shan large-leaf (Camellia sinensis var. assamica), plantation and old-garden leaf
processing: Bulang maocha is wet-piled in Menghai for roughly 45–60 days, usually to a medium-full degree, then dried, rested for months to lose the pile smell and pressed into cakes; the thick, bitter Bulang leaf is the preferred base for strong ripe tea.
harvest_season: Mostly spring and autumn plantation leaf, with old-garden lots from boutique makers; sold by production year.
appearance_dry: A dark-brown cake of thick, sturdy leaves with golden-tipped buds and a dense, slightly oily look.
appearance_liquor: Deep, dark red-brown, glossy and clear.
appearance_wet: Thick, leathery dark-brown leaves that stay intact and elastic after fermentation.
taste_profile: Powerful ripe tea: dark cocoa, dates and wood with a distinct bitter edge that the Bulang leaf keeps even after piling, a thick heavy body, a mineral earthiness and a long warm finish.

brewing.notes: Rinse twice with boiling water. Thick leaf takes boiling water and long late steeps; a clay pot softens the bitter edge. Air a young cake for a few weeks after breaking it.

vintage_note: Sold by production year and, for boutique lots, by village and tree class (Bulang gushu shu, Lao Man E shu), as cakes and bricks; the big Menghai factory's ripe blends have leaned on Bulang leaf for decades without naming it, so single-origin Bulang shu is mostly a 2010s-onward product. Young (1–3 years) it is strong and still carries pile smell; 4–10 years is the sweet spot where the bitterness has rounded into dark chocolate; aged examples beyond fifteen years are mostly unlabelled factory cakes. Supply is 2010–2025 and mostly Menghai- or Kunming-dry; the leaf's body means it tolerates Guangdong humidity well.
description:
Bulang shu is ripe pu-erh fermented from the thick, bitter leaf of Bulang Mountain in Menghai County, the same material that makes the most powerful raw tea in Yunnan. Fermentation tames most of the bitterness, but the body and a trace of that bite survive, which is why Bulang has been the preferred base for strong ripe tea since the Menghai factory's early days, and why boutique makers now press single-village Bulang shu, including the famously bitter Lao Man E.

The maocha is wet-piled in Menghai, usually to a medium-full degree so that the leaf keeps some character, dried, rested for months to lose the pile smell, then pressed into cakes. Old-garden lots are fermented in small batches, often off the ground in baskets or boxes, and sold with the village and tree class stated.

In the cup Bulang shu is the dark end of ripe tea: cocoa, dates and wood with a clear bitter edge, a heavy thick body, a mineral earthiness and a long warm finish. It is more of a tea than the soft, sweet Lincang style of shu and it pairs well with food. Boiling water, two rinses and a clay pot; young cakes benefit from airing and from a few years of patience.

It is sold by production year, as factory blends that quietly include it and as boutique cakes that advertise it, with gushu lots priced accordingly. The 'Bulang' label guarantees a style rather than a hillside, and a fair proportion of 'Bulang shu' is county-wide Menghai plantation leaf; the thick leathery wet leaf and the bitter edge are what to look for. Lao Man E shu is the extreme version for people who like their ripe tea with teeth.

If you find most shu bland, this is the one to try; if you find it too strong, a Lincang shu is the gentle opposite.
name_ru: Шу Пуэр с горы Бу Лан
history:
This is ripe pu-erh named for its leaf, which comes from Bulang Mountain in Menghai County, an area better known for strong raw tea. Tea drinkers commonly say that Bulang leaf has long gone into Menghai ripe blends without being named on the wrapper, though that is hard to document in detail.

Cakes sold under the Bulang name are a recent, boutique way of presenting the tea. Little is documented about who pressed the first of them, and the label usually describes a style more reliably than a hillside.
